title: stacks, queues, deques, and priority-agnostic worklists
concepts: A stack exposes last-in, first-out access; a queue exposes first-in, first-out access, so each is an abstract data type whose contract is separate from its implementation.
Array-backed stacks use a top index and grow dynamically; linked stacks use nodes, with memory locality and allocation behavior differing between representations.
A circular array queue reuses freed slots by wrapping head and tail indices; a linked queue can maintain head and tail references for constant-time enqueue and dequeue.
A deque supports insertion and removal at both ends and can model either a stack or a queue, while not automatically guaranteeing efficient middle access.
Two stacks can simulate a queue by transferring elements only when the outgoing stack is empty; each item moves a bounded number of times, giving amortized constant-time operations.
A queue can simulate a stack with rotation or multiple queues, but the chosen operation costs depend on which structure operations the design makes cheap.
Expression parsing, nested delimiter matching, undo histories, breadth-first traversal, and task buffering use ordering constraints that naturally fit stacks or queues.
A priority queue is ordered by priority rather than arrival time and is a separate structure, typically heap-backed; it is outside this FIFO/LIFO topic.
Empty-structure behavior, capacity growth, overflow policy for fixed-capacity buffers, and amortized versus worst-case costs must be made explicit in an implementation.
